entities.name: Ariobarzanes II of Cappadocia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ariobarzanes II of Cappadocia, whose reign is marked by a period of increasing Roman influence and internal instability in the Anatolian kingdom, assumed the throne around 63/62 BCE, succeeding his father, Ariobarzanes I Philoromaios. Despite the initial summary's conflicting dates, historical consensus places his assassination around 51/50 BCE, not 100 BCE. His brief tenure was characterized by the delicate balancing act required to maintain Cappadocia's autonomy amidst the burgeoning power of the Roman Republic, specifically through the patronage of Pompey the Great. His rule occurred during the late Hellenistic period, a pivotal era when independent kingdoms in Anatolia were steadily absorbed into the Roman sphere.

During his time as king, Ariobarzanes II continued the pro-Roman policy established by his father, a necessity for the survival of Cappadocia as a buffer state. He faced significant challenges from internal factions and rival claimants, notably his brother Ariarathes, and the ongoing machinations of Pontus and Armenia, though their direct threat had diminished after Roman victories. He was compelled to seek financial aid from Rome, incurring debts that further entangled Cappadocia in Roman affairs. His reign saw the continued construction and maintenance of infrastructure, albeit under financial strain, and the preservation of Hellenistic culture within the Cappadocian court, even as political independence waned.
